overview.title: Nature And Functions Of A Stock Exchange
overview.definition: A stock exchange is an organized and regulated financial marketplace where buyers and sellers trade existing shares, debentures, and other securities, providing vital liquidity, capital formation, and price discovery to the economy.
overview.importanceInUpsc: Frequently tested in UPSC Prelims regarding regulatory bodies (SEBI), capital market instruments, and secondary market mechanisms. In Mains (GS Paper III - Indian Economy), it forms the bedrock of resource mobilization, corporate governance, and inclusive growth.
learningOutcomes: Master foundational concepts and mechanisms of Nature And Functions Of A Stock Exchange.
Evaluate spatial distribution, institutional frameworks, and policy dimensions.
Apply high-yield mnemonics to solve tricky Prelims and Mains questions.
prerequisites: Difference between Primary and Secondary Markets

sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Economic Barometer**: A stock exchange acts as a leading economic indicator, reflecting the health, stability, and future expectations of an economy through indices like **Sensex** and **Nifty**.
• **Continuous Market & Liquidity**: It provides a ready and continuous market for the sale and purchase of securities, transforming illiquid long-term investments into liquid assets for investors.
• **Price Discovery Mechanism**: Prices of securities are determined through the interplay of free-market **demand and supply forces**, ensuring transparent valuation based on corporate fundamentals.
• **Safety of Transactions**: All dealings are regulated under strict statutory frameworks (Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and SEBI Act, 1992), minimizing counterparty and systemic default risks.

items.definition: The structural transition of a stock exchange from a mutually-owned association (controlled by brokers) to a shareholder-owned corporate entity, eliminating conflict of interest.
An institution that guarantees the settlement of trades, acts as a legal counterparty to both buyer and seller, and mitigates settlement risk.
Regulatory mechanism implemented by SEBI (at 10%, 15%, and 20% index movements) to halt trading temporarily and curb panic-driven market volatility.

Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act (SCRA) 1956; SEBI Act 1992; P.J. Nayak Committee on governance of boards; Dr. Bimal Jalan Committee on ownership and governance of market infrastructure institutions.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Financial Capitals**: Mumbai hosts India's primary financial infrastructure (BSE, NSE, SEBI HQ), serving as the epicenter of capital mobilization.
• **Regional Exchanges**: Historically featured cities like Kolkata, Chennai, and Ahmedabad, most of which exited operations or transformed into regional trading platforms due to the rise of nationwide electronic exchanges (NSE/BSE).

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: High-frequency trading (HFT) vulnerabilities, algorithmic trading risks, cyber security threats, and systemic contagion from global shocks.
• **Policy Interventions**: T+1 settlement cycles introduced by SEBI, enhanced surveillance measures (GSM/ASM), and tightening of algorithmic trading guardrails.

items.title: Mnemonic for Core Functions of Stock Exchange
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "L-P-S-E-F" (Liquidity, Pricing, Safety, Economic barometer, Facility for speculation/investment).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Liquidity provision, Price discovery, Safety of transactions, Economic indicator, Facilitating capital flow.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Quickly verifies statements in multi-statement MCQs regarding whether a function belongs to a stock exchange.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Secondary market = Trading existing shares (No fresh capital to company). Primary market = Issuing new shares (Fresh capital to company).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often frames statements claiming that 'buying shares on a stock exchange directly increases a company's working capital.' This is INCORRECT because secondary market transactions only transfer ownership between investors; the issuing company receives no fresh capital.

Mains Value Addition: In answers related to investment, financial inclusion, or economic growth, emphasize how robust stock exchange mechanisms reduce the cost of capital, channel household savings into productive assets, and strengthen corporate governance standards.

keyTakeaways: Stock exchanges serve as the secondary market providing liquidity, continuous pricing, and safe settlement mechanisms for existing securities.
Regulatory oversight by SEBI under the SCRA 1956 ensures market integrity, investor protection, and systemic stability through demutualization and circuit breakers.
Transactions on stock exchanges do not inject fresh capital into corporations, distinguishing the secondary market from the primary market.
